title: Synapse gosync-worker
description: Go reimplementation of Synapse's classic /sync worker: traffic, long-poll occupancy, replication health and the one write it makes.

list.name: job
list.label: Job
list.description: Populated from the data, so any scrape job name works.

list.name: endpoint
list.label: Endpoint
list.description: sync, events, initial_sync, room_initial_sync -- plus `unknown` for anything that reached the router without being annotated.

list.name: bucket
list.label: Bucket
list.description: Range window for rate() and histogram_quantile(). rate() needs two samples, so with a 15s scrape 30s is the floor; a single client generates one request every 30 seconds, which is why the default is 5m rather than the floor. `auto` divides the dashboard's time range into 30 buckets and never goes below 30s, which is the right choice when zooming out past a day -- a fixed 5m window over a week asks Prometheus for thousands of points per series and the panel gets slow long before it gets unreadable.

panels.title: Requests
panels.description: Requests served per second, all four endpoints.

panels.title: 5xx ratio
panels.description: Share of requests that failed on our side. Anything sustained above zero is a bug, not load. Reads 0 rather than "No data" when it has never happened: for a panel whose healthy value is zero, those two must not look the same.

targets.expr: (sum(rate(gosync_requests_total{endpoint=~"$endpoint", job=~"$job", status=~"5.."}[$bucket])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min(sum(rate(gosync_requests_total{endpoint=~"$endpoint", job=~"$job"}[$bucket])) or vector(0), 0.0001)

panels.title: Long polls parked
panels.description: Clients currently waiting for something to happen. On a worker serving real clients this is the steady state: idle syncs, not idle CPU. Zero with clients connected means they are not reaching us.

panels.title: Replication
panels.description: The gauge that matters. While this is 0 the worker cannot report typing at all and its stream positions are only as fresh as the last database seed -- and /health will still say ok, because it does not check this.

panels.title: Database role
panels.description: 1 when the main pool's role cannot write. To-device deletion uses a separate role and a separate pool, so this staying at 1 is expected even with to_device enabled.

panels.title: Version
panels.description: Tag the running image was built from.

panels.title: Requests by endpoint
panels.description: Element Web drives /sync almost exclusively; the three legacy endpoints should be flat at zero unless something is deliberately calling them.

panels.title: Duration percentiles
panels.description: READ THIS CAREFULLY: a /sync that waits the client's full timeout and returns nothing is a SUCCESS, and it lands at 30s. High percentiles here are the normal shape of a healthy long-polling endpoint. What matters is the LOW end -- an initial sync or a sync with news should be well under a second.

panels.title: Outcomes
panels.description: served / refused / client_gone. A client hanging up mid-long-poll is ORDINARY for /sync -- Element does it on every navigation -- and is deliberately not counted as an error.

panels.title: Status codes
panels.description: 401 and 403 are the client's problem; 5xx is ours. A burst of 502 means whoami could not reach Synapse -- the worker refuses to guess rather than logging clients out.

panels.title: Long polls parked
panels.description: Should track the number of connected clients, and should return to that level after every wakeup. A sawtooth that never comes back down is a leak.

panels.title: Duration distribution
panels.description: Expect two clusters on a live worker: fast responses at the bottom, and a band at the client's timeout where idle long polls expire. A spreading middle is where trouble shows.

panels.title: Requests by status and endpoint
panels.description: The same counter split both ways, for when one endpoint misbehaves and the others do not.

panels.title: Token cache
panels.description: Cached token verdicts. Bounded by auth.max_entries.

panels.title: Rejections
panels.description: Tokens Synapse said no to. Reads 0 rather than "No data" when it has never happened: for a panel whose healthy value is zero, those two must not look the same.

panels.title: Whoami unavailable
panels.description: The one to watch: Synapse could not be asked. The worker answers 502 and NEVER 401, because refusing a valid token would log real clients out. Sustained non-zero means the whoami socket is wrong or the client-API worker is down. Reads 0 rather than "No data" when it has never happened: for a panel whose healthy value is zero, those two must not look the same.

panels.title: Verdicts
panels.description: accepted / rejected / missing / unavailable.

panels.title: Deleted in range
panels.description: Messages this worker has deleted from device_inbox over the dashboard's time range. This is the only write it makes. Zero with an encrypted client connected means to_device is disabled -- and that client will never receive room keys.

panels.title: Deletion rate
panels.description: Deletion is bounded by each client's own `since`, so this should track how fast messages arrive for the devices syncing here. A rate far above that means something is acknowledging on a client's behalf.

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: A parked long poll costs no CPU. This should be near zero between wakeups.

panels.title: Resident memory
panels.description: Watch the trend across days, not the value. The state caches fill as rooms are touched and then plateau; a line that never flattens is the thing to report.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: Roughly two per parked long poll plus the replication subscriber. Should fall back when clients disconnect -- if it does not, that is a leak.

panels.title: Open files
panels.description: One per connected client, plus the database pool and the Redis connection.

panels.title: Memory
panels.description: Days, not minutes: this is the panel a soak is for.

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: Fraction of one core. A parked long poll costs nothing, so this should sit near zero between wakeups and rise while a sync is built. Sustained load with no traffic means work is happening off the request path -- the typing hot loop looked exactly like that, at 15%. GC is drawn alongside so a rise can be attributed: the Go client does not export a user/system split on Linux, so that is not available here.

panels.title: Goroutines and waiters
panels.description: These two should move together. Goroutines climbing while waiters do not is a leak in something other than the long poll.

panels.title: Queries per request
panels.description: Database round trips per client request. THE number this worker is optimised for: its cost is round trips, not database seconds. A quiet incremental sync should sit near 18; it was 688 before the query work.

panels.title: Query rate
panels.description: Queries issued to Synapse's PostgreSQL, per second.

panels.title: Cache hit rate
panels.description: MISLEADING ON ITS OWN. A disarmed cache reports neither hits nor misses, so 'no data' here means the caches are switched off or replication is down -- not that they are useless. Read Caches armed beside it.

panels.title: Caches armed
panels.description: How many derived caches are serving. Anything below 7 means replication is down and the caches are refusing to answer rather than guessing. Alert on this, not on the hit rate.

panels.title: Cache purges
panels.description: Rows on Synapse's caches stream treated as destructive. Should be at or near ZERO. That stream carries a row every couple of seconds, almost all of it about caches this worker does not hold; an earlier build treated every row as destructive and emptied the state caches continuously, costing 4,910 extra queries on one initial sync. Reads 0 rather than 'No data' when there have been none, so a blank panel means the metric is missing, not that the count is zero.

panels.title: State cache entries
panels.description: Immutable state-group caches. These hold state groups, which never change, so they are always on -- unlike the derived caches.

panels.title: Queries by store method
panels.description: Which store method is talking to the database. The top entry is the next thing worth removing; a single method dominating usually means it is being asked once per room.

panels.title: Cache hits and misses
panels.description: Per cache. A cache with misses and no hits is either newly armed (a guarded cache does not answer until replication has caught up to the token) or genuinely useless -- check its entry count before concluding.

panels.title: Cache entries
panels.description: Entries held per derived cache. A cache pinned flat at its configured bound is evicting; raise it or accept the misses.

panels.title: Cache evictions
panels.description: Evictions per cache. Sustained eviction on room_summary means the account has more rooms than the cache is sized for.

panels.title: Caches stream, by action
panels.description: What we did with each row on Synapse's caches replication stream. 'ignored' should dominate: those rows concern caches this worker does not hold. 'purge' should be flat at zero.

panels.title: Row rate
panels.description: Replication rows received per second, every stream. This worker follows the whole channel, so this is the homeserver's activity, not ours.

panels.title: Global rows
panels.description: Share of rows that name neither a room nor a user, and therefore wake EVERY parked client. This is the panel that found the caches stream doing it about once a second: 94 of 95 global rows were that one stream, waking every client to recompute a sync that was always empty. Streams that wake nobody by design are counted scope="silent" and are not in this number.

panels.title: Wakeups per row
panels.description: How many parked syncs the average replication row costs. Approaching the parked-client count means rows are waking everybody; near zero on an idle server is right.

panels.title: Wakeup rate
panels.description: Parked syncs woken per second. Each one recomputes a sync; most find nothing and park again.

panels.title: Rows by stream
panels.description: Which streams carry the traffic. presence dominates on a federated server and is correctly targeted at one user per row.

panels.title: Wakeups by stream
panels.description: Which streams actually cost us work. A stream high here but low in Rows by stream is waking many clients per row -- that is the shape to investigate.

panels.title: Rows by scope
panels.description: Stacked. 'global' wakes every parked client and should be a thin band; 'silent' is a stream that wakes nobody by design -- the caches stream, which carries Synapse's own invalidations and appears in no stream token.

panels.title: Gate horizon lag
panels.description: gosync_stream_cache_earliest_position subtracted from the stream's current position: how far back each cache can answer. THIS IS THE PANEL THAT MATTERS. A cache too small for its stream has this shrink towards zero; every question then falls below the horizon, every gate answers 'changed', and the queries come back with no error and no wrong answer. A flat line at 0 for a stream means its cache is doing nothing. membership is measured against the events position because it has no stream of its own -- it is fed by m.room.member rows. It and account_data are armed empty and start at 0 lag by design; they fill from live traffic.

panels.title: Queries the gates skipped
panels.description: The payoff, read from the queries that did NOT run. PresenceSince is the expensive one: a correlated subquery over presence_stream and current_state_events, 25ms warm and 430ms cold, previously run once per sync whether or not any presence had moved. Compare against the sync rate: on a quiet server most syncs should run neither.

panels.title: Stream cache hits and misses
panels.description: A 'hit' is a question answered from memory, whether the answer was 'changed' or 'unchanged' -- so a high hit rate means the cache is working, not that queries were skipped. Use the skipped-queries panel for that. Misses are questions that fell below the horizon.

panels.title: Entities and positions held
panels.description: Positions is what the size bound limits, not entities: one stream position can name many rooms. Positions sitting exactly at the configured size means the cache is full and evicting.

panels.title: Evictions, and gates armed
panels.description: Evictions raise the horizon, which is how a too-small cache quietly stops working -- read this alongside the horizon-lag panel. Armed drops to 0 when replication is lost, at which point every gate answers 'changed' and the worker behaves exactly as it did before these caches existed. It also reads 0 for a cache configured to hold nothing, deliberately: that is indistinguishable from disarmed to every caller.

panels.title: Responses by outcome
panels.description: THE PANEL TO CHECK FIRST. `immediate` means there was news without waiting, `woken` means a parked poll was woken by it, `timed_out` means it waited to the deadline with nothing. A worker answering `immediate` on nearly every request has a broken emptiness rule, not a busy server -- on 2026-09-03 any present extension counted as news, so the long poll never waited and SchildiChat was answered about ten times a second per connection. Healthy shape: `woken` and `timed_out` carrying the traffic, `immediate` only as often as clients start new connections.

panels.title: Rooms per response
panels.description: After the first response for a connection, a quiet poll should describe ZERO rooms. A steady stream of full windows means every response re-sends everything, which is the difference between a sliding sync and a very expensive /sync.

panels.title: Connection-store writes
panels.description: This endpoint is the only one that writes. The write is proportional to the connection's ROOM COUNT rather than to what changed, because each new position copies the previous one's rows forward -- measured at ~725 stream rows plus ~248 room-config rows per position for a 654-room connection, times the three connections Element X holds per device. A quiet poll should write nothing: compare positions_minted against the response rate, and if they track each other the 'reuse the position when nothing changed' short-circuit has stopped working.

panels.title: Connection store size
panels.description: Small by design: reading a position deletes the other positions on its connection, and the reaper removes connections nobody uses. A row count that climbs steadily means one of those two has stopped -- `reaped` flat at zero for days is the reaper, and positions far above connections is the prune. Neither is visible any other way. `store_up` at 0 means the last scrape could not reach the database, so the other numbers here are stale.

panels.title: Response size
panels.description: A client controls its own window and required_state, so it controls this almost entirely. The expensive failure here is not a slow query but a client asking for a thousand rooms with ["*","*"].

panels.title: Unknown positions
panels.description: M_UNKNOWN_POS is a supported path, not an error: the client starts a fresh connection. A steady trickle is normal (9.3% of live requests already begin with no connection state). A SPIKE is not -- every connected client re-bootstrapping at once is what a schema change or a misconfigured reaper looks like.
